explanations.answer: The days of mourning for his father
explanations.explanation: Esau says in his heart, "The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob." (Gen 27:41) So the thing he's waiting on is the days of mourning for Isaac. I think this is a heavy one, baker, and it's okay to just sit with that. The text says Esau held a grudge because of the blessing (Gen 27:41).

explanations.answer: The end of the harvest season
explanations.explanation: Harvest never comes up in this passage. Esau says in his heart, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob.” (Gen 27:41) The wait he names is the days of mourning for his father. I think this one hurts, baker.

explanations.answer: The return of his hunting party
explanations.explanation: No hunting party shows up in these verses. What Esau says in his heart is, “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then I will kill my brother Jacob.” (Gen 27:41) That's the wait he names. I think this is a heavy one, baker.

Rebekah tells Jacob, “So now, my son, obey my voice and flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran.” (Gen 27:43) The one she names is her own brother Laban. She says this right after she sends for Jacob and tells him about Esau's plot (Gen 27:42). I think this is a heavy moment, baker.

Deborah isn't in these verses at all. Rebekah tells Jacob, “So now, my son, obey my voice and flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran.” (Gen 27:43) Laban is the name she gives, and he is her brother. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'm glad the text is clear on this part.
Eliezer doesn't show up in this passage. Rebekah says, "…flee at once to my brother Laban in Haran." (Gen 27:43) Laban is her own brother. The text gives no other name for the trip.

Rebekah says, “Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides…” (Gen 27:44) Fury is the word she uses. The stay is for a while, until that fury subsides. I think this is a heavy one, baker, since it sits right beside Esau's plot.
Hunger isn't the word in the verse. Rebekah says, "Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides…" (Gen 27:44) Fury is what she wants to see settle. Hunger never makes the list.

Fever isn't the word in the verse. Rebekah says, “Stay with him for a while, until your brother’s fury subsides…” (Gen 27:44) The word is fury. That's the thing she wants to see subside, and I think it's a heavy thing to be waiting on.

Rebekah says nothing like that. She tells Jacob, “Then I will send for you and bring you back from there.” (Gen 27:45) She is the one who will send for him. I think this is a heavy moment, baker, and her plan includes his return.

Right, and here's what the text says. Rebekah tells Jacob, "Then I will send for you and bring you back from there." (Gen 27:45) The plan is for her to send for him. Jacob isn't left to find his own way home.

Rebekah says, "I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women." (Gen 27:46) Hittite is the word she uses. She goes on to ask what good her life is if Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them. The text doesn't say more about why, so I won't guess.

Egyptian isn't the word here. Rebekah says, “I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women.” (Gen 27:46) The women she names are Hittite. She also asks, “If Jacob takes a Hittite wife from among them, what good is my life?” (Gen 27:46)
Philistine doesn't show up in this verse. Rebekah says to Isaac, "I am weary of my life because of these Hittite women." (Gen 27:46) The word she picks is Hittite. The text keeps it that simple.

Yes, baker. "So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him." (Gen 28:1) Think about that for a second. Jacob walks in after what he did in Genesis 27:35 and walks out blessed. That's the text, plain as dough.
The text says the opposite. "So Isaac called for Jacob and blessed him." (Gen 28:1) Jacob had taken Esau's blessing deceitfully (Gen 27:35). Even so, this verse says Isaac blessed him.

Isaac commands him, "Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women…" (Gen 28:1) That's the command, word for word. Then he points Jacob toward Laban's daughters (Gen 28:2). The direction comes with the rule.

explanations.answer: Don't marry until Esau forgives you
explanations.explanation: Isaac says nothing about Esau forgiving anybody. His command is, "Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women…" (Gen 28:1) It's about who Jacob marries. Esau's anger isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: Marry before your mother sends for you
explanations.explanation: There's no race against Rebekah in this verse. Isaac commands, "Do not take a wife from the Canaanite women…" (Gen 28:1) Rebekah does say she will send for Jacob later, but that's about bringing him home (Gen 27:45). Isaac's command is about the Canaanite women.

Isaac blesses Jacob, “And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants…” (Gen 28:4) So Isaac asks God to give Jacob and his descendants the blessing of Abraham. Abraham is Isaac's father (Gen 25:19). That's the name in the verse, baker.

Noah isn't named in this blessing. Isaac says, “And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants…” (Gen 28:4) Isaac asks God to give that blessing to Jacob and his descendants. Abraham is the name in the verse, and he's Isaac's father (Gen 25:19).

Adam doesn't come up here. Isaac says, "And may He give the blessing of Abraham to you and your descendants…" (Gen 28:4) Abraham is the name in the verse, and he's Isaac's father (Gen 25:19). The blessing stays in the family.

explanations.answer: The land where he lives as a foreigner
explanations.explanation: Isaac's blessing says Jacob may "…possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham." (Gen 28:4) That's the ending of the blessing. It's land that God gave to Abraham. Isaac hands it on in words.

explanations.answer: The wells his father dug in Gerar
explanations.explanation: Wells aren't in this blessing. Isaac says Jacob may "…possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham." (Gen 28:4) The blessing ends on land, and nothing else. Gerar doesn't get a mention.

explanations.answer: The flocks of his uncle Laban
explanations.explanation: Laban's flocks aren't in the blessing. Isaac says Jacob may "…possess the land where you dwell as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham." (Gen 28:4) That's the end of it. It's about the land, not Laban's herds.

The text says Esau, "…seeing that his father Isaac disapproved of the Canaanite women…" went to Ishmael and married Mahalath. (Gen 28:8-9) Mahalath is Ishmael's daughter. Ishmael is Abraham's son. So Esau goes back into the family for a wife.

Lot isn't in these verses. The text says Esau "…went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael…" (Gen 28:9) That's the household he goes to. Lot never comes up.

Nahor doesn't appear here. The text says Esau "…went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham’s son Ishmael…" (Gen 28:9) The man he visits is Ishmael. That's the whole answer.
The text says Esau married Mahalath "…in addition to the wives he already had." (Gen 28:9) In addition, baker, not instead of. Nobody got replaced. Mahalath was added to the list.
Yes, and the text says it directly. Esau married Mahalath "…in addition to the wives he already had." (Gen 28:9) She wasn't a replacement. She joined the wives he already had.

The text says, “…taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep.” (Gen 28:11) A stone, baker. No fluff, no thread count, no pillow menu. That's the bedding the verse gives.

Logs aren't in the verse. The text says, "…taking one of the stones from that place, he put it under his head and lay down to sleep." (Gen 28:11) It was a stone under his head. A hard pillow, I think.
No branches here. The text says Jacob took "…one of the stones from that place…" and put it under his head. (Gen 28:11) That's what he lay down on. I think a stone makes for a firm night.

"…Jacob had a dream about a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven…" (Gen 28:12) Bottom on the earth, top reaching heaven. That's what he sees while he sleeps. A very tall ladder, baker.
The dream isn't about a tower. The text says it was "…a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven…" (Gen 28:12) A ladder is what Jacob sees. That's the word the verse uses.
A mountain isn't in the dream. The verse says, "…a ladder that rested on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven…" (Gen 28:12) So it's a ladder, resting on the earth. The text stays with that.
The text says, “…God’s angels were going up and down the ladder.” (Gen 28:12) Up and down, both directions. That's what Jacob sees in the dream. Busy ladder, baker.
Prophets aren't on the ladder. The text says, "…God’s angels were going up and down the ladder." (Gen 28:12) Angels are the ones climbing. That's the word in the verse.
Priests don't show up in this dream. The text says, "…God’s angels were going up and down the ladder." (Gen 28:12) Angels, going up and down. That's the whole picture.

The LORD says, “I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie.” (Gen 28:13) Jacob is lying on the very ground being promised. The promise is for him and his descendants. That's a lot to hear in the middle of a night's sleep, baker.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says, "I will give you and your descendants the land on which you now lie." (Gen 28:13) The promise is about the very ground under Jacob. It's for him and his descendants.

The LORD says much bigger than that. "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring." (Gen 28:14) All the families of the earth, baker. That's a long way past one household.

Right, and here's what the text says. The LORD says, "All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your offspring." (Gen 28:14) That's all the families, not only Jacob's. The promise reaches wide, like dust spreading in every direction.

explanations.answer: To be with him and bring him back
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, "…I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land." (Gen 28:15) Wherever he goes, he's not going alone. And there's a trip home built into the promise. That's a lot to hear while lying on a rock.

explanations.answer: To make the road short and easy
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't say the road will be short or easy. He says, "…I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land." (Gen 28:15) The promise is that He'll be with Jacob and bring him back. That's what the text gives.

explanations.answer: To soften Esau's heart right away
explanations.explanation: Esau doesn't come up in what the LORD says. He says, "…I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land." (Gen 28:15) The promise is His company and a return to the land. Nothing about Esau's heart is mentioned.

The text says otherwise. Jacob wakes and “…he was afraid…” (Gen 28:17) Then he says, “How awesome is this place!” (Gen 28:17) Afraid is the word the text uses, so I think calm isn't the right picture, baker.

Right, and here's what the text says. “…he was afraid…” (Gen 28:17) Jacob had just said, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I was unaware of it.” (Gen 28:16) So he's afraid, not calm, and he calls the place awesome.

explanations.answer: Sets it up as a pillar and pours oil on it
explanations.explanation: The text says, “…Jacob took the stone that he had placed under his head, and he set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…” (Gen 28:18) The stone he slept on becomes the pillar. Same stone, new job, baker. He does this early the next morning.

explanations.answer: Carries it with him all the way to Haran
explanations.explanation: The stone stays where it is. The text says Jacob "…set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…" (Gen 28:18) No hauling it down the road. It's set up in place.

explanations.answer: Builds an altar and offers a sacrifice on it
explanations.explanation: No altar or sacrifice is mentioned here. The text says Jacob "…set it up as a pillar. He poured oil on top of it…" (Gen 28:18) A pillar with oil is what he makes. The verse sticks to that.

explanations.answer: Food to eat and clothes to wear
explanations.explanation: Jacob's vow goes on, “…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…” (Gen 28:20) That's another IF in the vow, baker. The list is food and clothes. Simple things.

explanations.answer: Gold and silver for the road
explanations.explanation: Gold and silver aren't on Jacob's list. His vow says, “…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…” (Gen 28:20) The list is just food and clothes. No treasure chest in the vow, baker.

explanations.answer: Servants and camels for the trip
explanations.explanation: Servants and camels don't appear in the vow. Jacob says, “…if He will provide me with food to eat and clothes to wear…” (Gen 28:20) That's what he names. It's food and clothes, baker, plain and short.
Jacob says, “…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.” (Gen 28:22) One out of ten is the amount in the vow. It's a promise about all that God gives him. The word is tenth, baker.
Half is a lot bigger than what he says. Jacob says, “…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.” (Gen 28:22) A tenth is the amount in the verse, baker. Not half.
A third isn't the number here. Jacob says, “…of all that You give me I will surely give You a tenth.” (Gen 28:22) The word is tenth. That's the amount he names, baker.
